hints: Think about the word hybridoma, it is a hybrid of two cells. One partner must provide the ability to make the exact antibody you want.
Recall which lymphocyte secretes antibodies, and which partner cell can divide forever in culture to keep producing them.
walkthrough:
**What does a hybridoma need to do?**

Think of it like building the perfect factory. You need the instructions to make one specific antibody, plus a machine that never stops dividing.

No single normal cell can do both jobs alone.

**Who makes the antibody?**

Plasma cells, which develop from activated B-lymphocytes, are the cells that secrete antibodies. T-lymphocytes never secrete antibodies, they are for cell-mediated immunity.

So one parent must be an antibody-producing B-lymphocyte from an immunised mouse.

**Who provides endless division?**

Normal B-lymphocytes die quickly in culture. Tumour cells, specifically myeloma cells, divide indefinitely.

Fuse them together and you get a hybridoma: B-lymphocyte specificity + tumour cell immortality, which makes monoclonal antibodies non-stop.

options.A: Stem cells can divide a lot, but they do not make the specific antibody. You need the B-lymphocyte for antibody production and a tumour cell for immortality.
options.B: T-lymphocytes do not secrete antibodies, and stem cells are not used in this fusion. This combination gives neither specificity nor the hybridoma property.
options.C: Correct. The B-lymphocyte provides production of the single specific antibody, and the tumour (myeloma) cell provides the ability to divide indefinitely in culture.
options.D: Tumour cells are correct for endless division, but T-lymphocytes do not make antibodies, so this fusion could never produce monoclonal antibodies.
